title: Designing a frontend that can grow
excerpt: A practical way to separate routes, features, shared components, and content before a project becomes difficult to change.
author: Starter Team
content: A scalable frontend is less about having many folders and more about giving each kind of code a predictable home. Routes should describe URLs and compose screens. Features should own domain-specific sections, while shared components stay unaware of individual pages.

Keeping content in typed data files is useful for prototypes and content-driven sites. It gives teams a CMS-like boundary without introducing infrastructure too early, and the same types can later describe API responses.
The best starter is intentionally ordinary. It establishes accessibility, responsive layout, metadata, and error states once, then stays out of the way as the product develops.

title: Practical SEO with the App Router
excerpt: Build canonical metadata, social previews, structured data, robots rules, and sitemaps into the project foundation.
author: Starter Team
content: SEO works best as part of route composition instead of a final checklist. Static pages can export metadata directly, while dynamic routes can create metadata from the same record used to render the page.

Canonical URLs prevent ambiguity, Open Graph metadata improves link previews, and structured data gives crawlers explicit information about the page. Each one solves a different problem, so a complete starter includes all three.
Sitemaps should be generated from the same source as route params. This prevents published detail pages from quietly disappearing from discovery when content changes.

title: Using motion with restraint
excerpt: Small animation primitives can improve hierarchy and feedback without turning a product interface into a presentation.
author: Starter Team
content: Interface motion should clarify what changed, where an element came from, or whether an action succeeded. When animation has no communicative purpose, it quickly becomes visual noise.
A small set of fade, slide, scale, stagger, and hover primitives covers most product needs. Keeping these effects local makes them easy to replace and keeps feature components readable.
Reduced-motion support is not an optional enhancement. Animation utilities should respect the system preference automatically so every feature gets the correct behavior by default.
